definition:
The resurrection of Jesus is the church's confession that on the third day after his crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, God raised Jesus of Nazareth from the dead in the same body that had been buried, now transformed and no longer subject to death. It is not a claim that his spirit survived, or that his teaching lived on, or that his followers found new courage. The tomb was empty because the body that lay in it had been made alive, and the risen Jesus was seen, heard, and touched by people who had known him before he died. Paul puts the whole faith on this one event: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). The resurrection vindicates Jesus as Lord and Messiah, seals the forgiveness won at the cross, defeats death, and is “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), the first sheaf of the harvest that will be the resurrection of all God's people. That wider harvest has its own study (Resurrection and the Last Things); this one concentrates on the risen Christ himself.

The New Testament uses two verbs. Egeirō means ‘to wake’ or ‘to raise up’, and it appears most often in the passive, ‘he was raised’, which puts the stress on God as the one who acted (Acts 2:24; Romans 4:25). Paul uses its perfect form, egēgertai, ‘he has been raised’, seven times in 1 Corinthians 15, a form that presents the raising as a completed act whose result stands. The second verb is anistēmi, ‘to stand up’ or ‘to rise’, with its noun anastasis, ‘resurrection’. In ordinary Greek anastasis could mean simply standing up, and a word's history does not settle its meaning; what matters is usage. In Jewish usage of Jesus' day, and in the pagan writers who denied it, ‘resurrection’ meant a dead person coming back to bodily life, not the survival of a soul. In the Hebrew Bible the key words are qum, ‘to arise’ (Isaiah 26:19), heqits, ‘to awake’ (Daniel 12:2), and chayah, ‘to live’ or ‘to come to life’ (Ezekiel 37:5).
ot:
The Old Testament rarely speaks of resurrection directly, and it is honest to say so. For much of Israel's history the dead went down to Sheol, the shadowy realm of the grave, and psalmists asked whether the dead could praise God at all. But the ground was laid early and deep, in the character of the God Israel worshiped. He is the one who says, “I bring death and I give life” (Deuteronomy 32:39), and Hannah sings that “He brings down to Sheol and raises up” (1 Samuel 2:6). He is the Creator who formed a man from dust and breathed life into him (Genesis 2:7), so that death, when it came through sin (Genesis 3:19), was an intrusion into his world and not its natural end. When Abraham took Isaac to Moriah and told his servants, “The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you” (Genesis 22:5), the letter to the Hebrews later reads the scene as faith that “God could raise the dead” (Hebrews 11:19). Elijah and Elisha each prayed over a dead boy who came back to life (1 Kings 17:21-22; 2 Kings 4:32-35), and a dead man thrown into Elisha's tomb “was revived and stood up on his feet” (2 Kings 13:21). These were restorations to ordinary mortal life, not resurrection in the full sense, but they showed that death does not have the last word where God is present.

The Psalms press further. In Psalm 16 David trusts that God will not abandon him to the grave: “For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (Psalm 16:10). Peter and Paul both preach this verse as a prophecy of Christ, arguing that David himself died and was buried, so the promise found its full meaning in his descendant (Acts 2:25-31; 13:35-37). Psalm 49 says, “God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself” (Psalm 49:15), and Psalm 73 speaks of God who will “later receive me in glory” (Psalm 73:24). Job, in the depth of his suffering, declares, “I know that my Redeemer lives” and that “in my flesh I will see God” (Job 19:25-26). The Hebrew of Job 19:26 is notoriously difficult, and translators differ on whether Job expects to see God in his body or apart from it, so the verse is better read as a cry of hope than as a finished doctrine.

The prophets bring the hope into focus. Hosea calls Israel to return, trusting that “on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence” (Hosea 6:2). The verse speaks of the nation's restoration, but the Aramaic paraphrase known as Targum Jonathan rendered it as referring to the day of the resurrection of the dead, and many Christians have heard in it an anticipation of the third day. Isaiah's vision of the end promises that God “will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:8), a line Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 15:54, and then says outright, “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19). Ezekiel's valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37:1-14) is a vision of Israel's return from exile, “these bones are the whole house of Israel” (Ezekiel 37:11), yet its language of opened graves and breath entering bodies shows how naturally Israel's hope took the shape of bodily resurrection. Isaiah's Servant, who is ‘cut off’ and buried with the wicked, afterward “will see the light of life and be satisfied” (Isaiah 53:11) and “will prolong His days” (Isaiah 53:10), a pattern of death followed by vindication that the apostles read as fulfilled in Jesus.

The clearest Old Testament statement comes in Daniel, in a vision of a final time of distress: “And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2). Here resurrection is personal, bodily, and tied to judgment. In the centuries between the Testaments the hope grew stronger, especially under persecution. 2 Maccabees 7, written in the late second century BC, tells of a mother and her seven sons martyred under Antiochus IV who die confessing that God will raise them. By Jesus' day the Pharisees affirmed the resurrection and the Sadducees, the priestly party, denied it (Acts 23:8). What no Jewish group expected was that one man would be raised ahead of everyone else, in the middle of history. Resurrection was something that would happen to all the righteous together at the end of the age, as Martha says to Jesus: “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day” (John 11:24).
nt:
Jesus predicted his own death and resurrection repeatedly, and the Gospels record that his disciples did not understand. After Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi, “He began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and after three days rise again” (Mark 8:31), and the prediction returns in Mark 9:31 and 10:34. He offered his opponents only “the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matthew 12:39), and he spoke of the temple of his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again” (John 2:19). At the tomb of Lazarus he said, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25), turning Martha's hope for the last day toward his own person. John also records Jesus saying that he lays down his life “in order to take it up again” (John 10:17). The New Testament attributes the resurrection to the Father (Acts 2:24; Galatians 1:1), to the Son himself (John 10:18), and to the Spirit (Romans 8:11), the three persons of the one God acting together.

All four Gospels narrate the discovery of the empty tomb on the first day of the week, and all four make women the first witnesses (Matthew 28:1-10; Mark 16:1-8; Luke 24:1-12; John 20:1-18). That detail matters historically because women's testimony carried little weight in courts of the time; Josephus (Antiquities 4.219) reports that it was not accepted. The narratives differ in their details, the number of women, the number of angels, the order of appearances, in the way independent accounts of a startling event usually differ. The risen Jesus is not a ghost. He tells the frightened disciples, “Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see—for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have” (Luke 24:39), and he eats broiled fish in front of them (Luke 24:42-43). He shows Thomas the wounds, and Thomas answers with the highest confession in the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). Yet his body is also changed: he is not always recognized at first (Luke 24:16; John 20:14), he appears among disciples behind locked doors (John 20:19), and he “cannot die again” (Romans 6:9). Matthew records that the authorities spread the story that the disciples stole the body (Matthew 28:11-15), which assumes the tomb was in fact empty. Mark's Gospel in the oldest manuscripts, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, ends at 16:8 with the women's fear; verses 9 to 20 were added later, which is why English Bibles mark them.

The apostles' preaching in Acts is resurrection preaching. At Pentecost Peter announces, “God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches” (Acts 2:24), and concludes that God has made this Jesus “both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36). The apostles are chosen as witnesses of the resurrection (Acts 1:22), and in Athens Paul tells the philosophers that God has given proof of the coming judgment “by raising Him from the dead” (Acts 17:31), at which some began to mock. The oldest written account is 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, written around AD 53 to 55, where Paul hands on a summary he had himself received: that Christ died for our sins, “that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4), and that he appeared to Cephas, to the Twelve, to more than five hundred at once, to James, to all the apostles, and last to Paul. Most scholars, including many who do not share Christian faith, hold that Paul received this summary within a few years of the crucifixion.

The apostles then draw out what the event means. The resurrection declares who Jesus is: he “was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:4). It completes the work of the cross: he “was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification” (Romans 4:25). It gives new life now, since believers are united with him in his death and resurrection so that “we too may walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). It is the pledge of the future, for the Spirit who raised Jesus “will also give life to your mortal bodies” (Romans 8:11), and Christ “will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (Philippians 3:21). He is the beginning and “firstborn from among the dead” (Colossians 1:18), and his resurrection is the beginning of the new creation. Peter says God has given us “new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). The last book of the Bible opens with the risen Christ saying to John, “I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades” (Revelation 1:18).

keyTexts.why: Abraham offers Isaac, trusting God's promise. Hebrews 11:19 reads the scene as faith that God could raise the dead, and says Abraham received Isaac back from death in a figure.
The Holy One will not see decay. Peter (Acts 2) and Paul (Acts 13) preach this psalm as fulfilled in the resurrection of David's descendant.
Your dead will live; their bodies will rise. One of the Old Testament's plainest statements of bodily resurrection.
After his death the Servant will see the light of life and prolong his days. The pattern of suffering followed by vindication that the apostles saw fulfilled in Jesus.
Dry bones receive breath and stand up. A vision of Israel's restoration that shows how naturally Israel's hope took the shape of bodily life from the grave.
Many who sleep in the dust will awake, to everlasting life or to contempt. The clearest statement of personal, bodily resurrection in the Old Testament.
Jesus teaches that the Son of Man must be killed and after three days rise again. The first of his repeated predictions.
The risen Jesus shows his hands and feet and eats fish. The resurrection body is real flesh and bones, not a ghost.
Jesus appears behind locked doors, shows his wounds, and receives Thomas's confession, “My Lord and my God.” Continuity and transformation together.
The first Christian sermon. God raised the crucified Jesus and so made him both Lord and Christ.
Jesus was declared Son of God in power by the resurrection. The event reveals and vindicates who he is.
He was raised for our justification. The resurrection is God's verdict that the sacrifice of the cross was accepted.
Believers are united with Christ in his death and resurrection and walk in newness of life. The risen life begins now.
The earliest written list of witnesses, Paul's argument that the faith stands or falls with this event, and Christ as the firstfruits of the harvest.
The risen Christ holds the keys of Death and of Hades. The one who was dead is alive forever.

history:
The earliest Christian writers made the bodily reality of the resurrection a point they would not surrender. Ignatius of Antioch, writing to the church at Smyrna on his way to martyrdom around AD 110 (Smyrnaeans 3), insisted that Jesus was in the flesh even after the resurrection, against the Docetists, teachers who held that Christ only seemed to have a body. Justin Martyr, around AD 155, explained to the emperor that Christians gather on Sunday because it is the day on which God began creation and on which Jesus rose from the dead (First Apology 67); the first day of the week had become the Lord's Day (Revelation 1:10). Irenaeus of Lyons, in Against Heresies (about AD 180), answered Gnostic teachers who despised the body and spoke of a purely spiritual salvation, arguing that the God who made flesh will raise it, and Tertullian's On the Resurrection of the Flesh (early third century) pressed the same case. When Origen of Alexandria (about 185 to 254) described the resurrection body as a transformed body whose form carried continuity rather than its material particles, Methodius of Olympus wrote On the Resurrection against him, and the debate over how the raised body relates to the buried one continued for centuries. The pagan critic Celsus, as Origen reports in Against Celsus (about 248), dismissed the witnesses as a hysterical woman and deluded followers, an objection that shows the Christian claim was understood from the start as a claim about a body.

The creeds made the resurrection a confession every Christian repeats. The Old Roman Creed, the ancestor of the Apostles' Creed, confessed that on the third day he rose again from the dead. The Nicene Creed of 325, as expanded at Constantinople in 381, confesses that he suffered, was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures, words taken from 1 Corinthians 15:4. Easter itself was the church's oldest annual feast. Polycarp of Smyrna and Anicetus of Rome disagreed around 155 over whether to keep it on the date of the Passover or on Sunday, and the Council of Nicaea in 325 moved the churches toward a common Sunday celebration. Augustine's City of God (completed about 426), Book 22, defended the resurrection of Christ and of believers as the goal of all history. Thomas Aquinas devoted Summa Theologiae III, questions 53 to 56, to the resurrection of Christ, its qualities, its manifestation, and its causal power in the resurrection of others. The Reformers held the confession without dispute: the Heidelberg Catechism (1563, question 45) names three benefits of the resurrection, that it makes us share in the righteousness Christ won, that by his power we are raised to new life, and that it is a sure pledge of our own resurrection; the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 8.4) states that he rose on the third day with the same body in which he suffered.

The modern challenge came from the Enlightenment. The deist Thomas Woolston attacked the resurrection accounts in his Discourses on the Miracles of Our Saviour (1727 to 1729), and Gotthold Lessing published fragments by the late Hermann Samuel Reimarus (1774 to 1778), the last of which argued that the disciples stole the body. Rationalist scholars such as H. E. G. Paulus proposed that Jesus did not die but revived in the cool tomb; David Friedrich Strauss, in his Life of Jesus (1835), treated the accounts as myth and later criticized the revival theory as impossible. Rudolf Bultmann's essay New Testament and Mythology (1941) reinterpreted Easter as the rise of faith in the preached message rather than an event in the body of Jesus. Against this, Karl Barth, in Church Dogmatics IV/1 (1953), spoke of the resurrection as the Father's verdict on the obedience of the Son, a real event in time known through God's self-disclosure. Wolfhart Pannenberg's Jesus, God and Man (German 1964) argued that the resurrection is a historical event open to historical reasoning, and Jürgen Moltmann's Theology of Hope (1964) made it the ground of Christian hope for the world. N. T. Wright's The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003) argued at length that only an empty tomb and real appearances explain why Jews who expected a general resurrection at the end proclaimed that one man had already been raised. The Jewish scholar Pinchas Lapide, in The Resurrection of Jesus (German 1977, English 1983), concluded that the resurrection was a real historical event while not accepting Jesus as Messiah. Skeptical scholars such as Gerd Lüdemann have argued instead that the appearances were visionary experiences, and Dale Allison's Resurrecting Jesus (2005) weighed the evidence on both sides with unusual candor. The site's page on the person of Christ sets the resurrection within the church's wider confession about who Jesus is.

differ.view: Resurrection as public history, open to evidence
differ.body: Many theologians and apologists hold that the resurrection happened in the same public world as the crucifixion and can be investigated by the ordinary tools of historical reasoning. They point out that Paul himself lists witnesses, many still alive and available to be questioned (1 Corinthians 15:6), and that Luke speaks of “many convincing proofs” (Acts 1:3). Wolfhart Pannenberg, N. T. Wright, Gary Habermas, and William Lane Craig argue from facts most historians accept, such as the crucifixion, the burial, the empty tomb, the appearances, and the sudden rise of a movement proclaiming a crucified Messiah, to the resurrection as the best explanation. They hold that this does not replace faith but shows that faith is not a leap against the evidence, and that a faith which stands or falls on a public event must be willing to have the event examined.

differ.view: Resurrection as revelation received in faith
differ.body: Others, while fully affirming that Jesus rose bodily and the tomb was empty, hold that the resurrection is known through God's self-disclosure and the apostolic witness rather than established by historical method. Karl Barth held that the Easter event really happened in time but is the act of God that historical research, bound to what is analogous to ordinary experience, cannot capture or prove. Reformed theologians in the presuppositional tradition, such as Cornelius Van Til, argue that the unbeliever's standards of evidence are themselves part of what the gospel challenges. Defenders of this approach point out that the risen Jesus appeared only to those he chose (Acts 10:40-41) and blessed “those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29), and they fear that resting faith on a historian's probabilities makes it hostage to the latest scholarship.

differ.view: The resurrection body: material identity or transformed continuity
differ.body: All orthodox Christians confess that Jesus rose in the same body that was buried, and that the tomb was empty. They differ on how to describe the continuity between the body sown and the body raised, a question that affects how they speak of believers' future bodies too. One tradition, from Tertullian and Augustine through much medieval theology, stressed material identity: the very flesh is raised, restored and glorified. Another, drawing on Paul's image of a seed that dies and is given “a body as He has designed” (1 Corinthians 15:38), stresses transformation: the raised body is truly the same person's body, as the wounds of Jesus show, yet it is imperishable and “a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44), meaning a body wholly animated by the Spirit, not a body made of spirit. Many modern theologians hold both emphases together without claiming to explain the mechanism.

differ.view: Between cross and resurrection: the descent into hell
differ.body: The Apostles' Creed confesses that Christ descended into hell before rising, a clause that entered its Western form in the fourth and fifth centuries. Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox teaching understands this as Christ going to the realm of the dead to free the righteous who had died before him, the event depicted in Eastern icons of the resurrection, drawing on 1 Peter 3:18-20 and Ephesians 4:9. The Lutheran Formula of Concord (1577, Article 9) confesses that the whole Christ descended to hell, defeated the devil, and destroyed hell's power. John Calvin (Institutes 2.16.10) read the clause as the agony of God's judgment Christ endured in his suffering on the cross. Some evangelical theologians, such as Wayne Grudem, have argued that the clause should be understood simply as burial or be dropped. All agree that Christ truly died and on the third day truly rose.

errors:
The church has rejected every account that keeps the word ‘resurrection’ while removing the risen body. Docetism, which held that Christ only seemed to have a body, was answered already by Ignatius and by Luke's insistence on flesh and bones (Luke 24:39). Some at Corinth said “there is no resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:12), probably because Greek thought regarded the body as a prison the soul escapes, and Paul answered that if the dead are not raised, Christ has not been raised either. Hymenaeus and Philetus taught that the resurrection “has already occurred” (2 Timothy 2:18), turning it into a spiritual experience in the present, and Paul says they undermined the faith of some. Gnostic teachers in the second century spoke of a spiritual rising while despising the flesh, and Irenaeus answered that such a salvation abandons the world God made. Modern reinterpretations that make Easter the rise of the disciples' faith, the survival of Jesus' cause, or a symbol of renewal, whatever their intentions, say less than the New Testament says and less than the creeds confess. Explanations that Jesus did not really die, that the body was stolen, or that the disciples went to the wrong tomb have all been proposed and answered, and none accounts for the transformation of the witnesses, several of whom died rather than deny what they had seen.

There are also errors of emphasis within the church. The resurrection can be treated as a mere proof that Christianity is true and then set aside, when the New Testament treats it as the beginning of new creation and the power of new life (Romans 6:4). It can be collapsed into the immortality of the soul, as if Easter only showed that people go to heaven when they die; Oscar Cullmann's lecture Immortality of the Soul or Resurrection of the Dead? (delivered 1955, published 1958) argued that these are different hopes. And it can be preached as a happy ending that cancels the cross, when the risen Jesus still bears his wounds.
life:
If Jesus was raised, death is not the final word over anyone who belongs to him. That does not take away grief; Paul does not tell the Thessalonians not to grieve, only that they should not grieve “like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Christians bury their dead expecting to see them again, in bodies, in a renewed world. It also means the body matters now. A faith whose Lord rose bodily cannot treat the body as disposable or the material world as unimportant, and Paul draws exactly that conclusion: because the dead will be raised, “your labor in the Lord is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Work done in faith, care for the sick, justice for the poor, faithfulness in small things, is not lost.

The resurrection also changes how a person faces guilt and fear. The one who was raised is the one who was crucified for sins, and his rising is God's announcement that the debt is paid (Romans 4:25). Paul wanted to know “the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings” (Philippians 3:10), in that order, and Christians have found that the risen Christ meets them not by removing every trial but by giving life in the middle of it. Every Sunday gathering is a small Easter, kept on the first day of the week because that is the day the tomb was found empty. And for the skeptic, the resurrection is the place where the Christian claim is most exposed to testing. The apostles did not ask to be believed on the strength of their feelings; they named witnesses and a date.
questions: Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:14-19). Why does he stake everything on a single event rather than on Jesus' teaching or example?
The risen Jesus eats fish and shows his wounds, yet passes through locked doors and is not always recognized. What do these details teach about continuity and change in the resurrection body?
Romans 6:4 says believers already walk in newness of life because of the resurrection. What would it look like for that to shape an ordinary week, not only a funeral?
